lesson.title: Generate values with clear boundaries

lead.text: Start with the surveyor's first method. She begins at 0 and walks along the path in strides of 3 metres, putting a post in each time she pauses. NumPy has a function for exactly this, called arange, short for “array range”. It takes three numbers. The first says where to start and the second says where to stop. The third is the size of each step.

For her path that is np.arange(0, 12, 3). It gives 0, 3, 6 and 9, and nothing more. The 12 is missing because arange counts up from the start and quits before it reaches the stop value, so the stop is never part of the result. Her path does have a post at 12 metres, and arange has left it off the list.
Step through the two cases below. With one number, as in np.arange(5), that number is the stop. The start is 0 and the step is 1, so the last value is 4.

afterFigure.text: The second case starts at 2 and steps by 3, so it makes 2, 5, 8 and 11. The next value would be 14, which is beyond the stop at 12, so it ends at 11. The step does not have to be a whole number. np.arange(0, 2, 0.5) makes 0, 0.5, 1 and 1.5, and the 2 stays out. To count the values by hand, step up from the start and stop before you reach the stop value.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import numpy as np
values = np.arange(5)

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import numpy as np
values = np.arange(2, 12, 3)

lead.text: List the values the way arange makes them. Begin at the start and keep adding the step, and stop before you reach the stop value.

The surveyor would like a post at the end of the path as well, and she would rather say how many posts she has than how big each stride is. NumPy's linspace, short for “linear space”, works that way. It takes the first value, the last value and how many values to make. It spreads them evenly, with the first at the start and the last at the end.

np.linspace(0, 12, 5) gives 0, 3, 6, 9 and 12, so this time the end of the path is included. Nobody told linspace the gap between posts. It worked the gap out. Five posts have four gaps between them, one fewer than the number of posts, and the 12 metres are shared among those four gaps: 12 ÷ 4 = 3 metres each.
The figure asks for four posts along the same path, with and without the end. Step through both cases.

afterFigure.text: With four posts there are three gaps, so the first case spaces them 4 metres apart, at 0, 4, 8 and 12. The second case adds endpoint=False, which tells linspace to leave the last point out. The 12 metres are now shared among four gaps, so the posts stand at 0, 3, 6 and 9, which is what arange gave at the start. Left alone, linspace includes its end, while arange never includes its stop.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import numpy as np
values = np.linspace(0, 12, 4)

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import numpy as np
values = np.linspace(0, 12, 4, endpoint=False)

lead.text: The surveyor now wants to inspect one post picked at random. She numbers her five posts 1 to 5, and she needs the computer to choose among those numbers without any pattern she could predict.

NumPy does this with a random generator, an object that produces numbers that look unpredictable. You make one with np.random.default_rng(), and by habit it is stored in a name called rng. Asking it for whole numbers uses its integers method, so rng.integers(1, 6, size=3) draws three whole numbers, each somewhere from 1 to 5.

The size says how many numbers to draw, and leaving it out gives a single number. Run the same line again with a fresh generator and you get different numbers, much as a die gives a different face on each roll.

The two limits given to integers follow the rule that arange used. The low limit can come up and the high limit cannot. rng.integers(1, 6) can return 1, 2, 3, 4 or 5, and it can never return 6. That is why the surveyor, with posts numbered 1 to 5, had to write 6 as the high limit.

Stopping short of the high limit also makes counting easy. The number of different values on offer is the high limit minus the low limit, so rng.integers(1, 6) has 6 − 1 = 5 choices, one for each post. A call such as rng.integers(10, 13) offers 3 values: 10, 11 and 12. The 13 stays out.
The high limit is the one that is left out. Decide which limits would allow the last number you want to come up.
The high limit is left out, so every value the generator returns lies below it.

There is a snag for the surveyor. If her colleague runs the same code tomorrow, a fresh generator gives different posts and the two of them cannot compare notes. The fix is to hand the generator a starting number, called a seed, when you create it.

np.random.default_rng(21) always begins from the same place, so it hands out the same numbers in the same order every time the code runs. A different seed gives a different sequence that is just as fixed. Step through the two cases, where only the seed changes.

afterFigure.text: Both cases ask for six whole numbers from 1 to 6, and they differ only in the seed. Anyone who creates a generator with seed 21 and makes the same call gets 2, 5, 3, 4, 3 and 5. A seed is how an analysis shares its random choices so that other people can check them. It does not make the sample any fairer. A sample that leaves out part of the picture leaves it out every time the code is rerun.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(21)
draws = rng.integers(1, 7, size=6)

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(22)
draws = rng.integers(1, 7, size=6)

lead.text: Two generators are each created with the same seed and asked for four whole numbers from 0 to 9. Compare what they return.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.random.default_rng(9).integers(0, 10, 4)
b = np.random.default_rng(9).integers(0, 10, 4)
equal = np.array_equal(a, b)

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(9)
a = rng.integers(0, 10, 4)
b = rng.integers(0, 10, 4)
equal = np.array_equal(a, b)

lesson.orientation: Distinguish arange, linspace and reproducible random draws.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea with a new input.

blocks.text: A footpath across a park is 12 metres long, and a surveyor wants to take a reading at regular points along it. She puts a post in at the start of the path and another every 3 metres after that. When she reaches the far end she is not sure whether the post at exactly 12 metres belongs on her list.

How she asks decides what NumPy gives back. One way is to say how big each step is and let the numbers run until they reach the end. Another is to say how many posts she needs and let the spacing follow. The two ways treat the last number differently, which is exactly what she is worried about.
Later she wants to inspect a few posts chosen by chance, and she wants a colleague to be able to choose the very same ones tomorrow. NumPy can do that too.

intro.promise: By the end you'll count the values arange and linspace make, and say what a random seed does.

recap.keyIdea: arange stops before its stop value and linspace includes its end unless told otherwise. integers leaves out its high limit, and a seed makes a random sequence repeat.

blocks.text: You saw that np.arange(0, 12, 3) leaves the post at 12 metres off the list, while np.linspace(0, 12, 5) keeps it. You counted 4 values in np.arange(3, 15, 3) and found that two generators with the same seed differ in 0 positions.

recap.nextHook: Every array in this lesson was built by a rule or by a generator. Most data you will meet arrives some other way, as a file of rows and columns that people filled in, with names across the top and codes mixed in among the counts. The next lesson reads such a file into pandas and checks what came in.
